utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm going to be asking you a few questions, and I'm going to start by asking some questions just to establish really the limits of what you can testify about. It's right, isn't it, firstly that in your work you weren't involved in the selection of objects?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know why objects were chosen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it right that the technology which allowed you to listen in on conversations, that's not something which you know particularly how that worked technically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: We were involved in the final part of the job only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So, for example, you don't know how it came to be that cables or phone lines came into the SDB office. You simply know that you were able to listen in on conversations. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also right that you don't know whether the interception which you carried out was authorised at the high levels; it's something which you took for granted that any interception work you were doing had been authorised by the appropriate person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, as far as any technical expertise in radio or telephone equipment, that's not something which you have, is it, you're not a specialist in how those systems work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: No. I did not have any expertise of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, if I were to ask you about how it was actually possible to have a telephone conversation being relayed between Sarajevo, Tuzla, and Srebrenica, and whether that involved transmitters or radio, that is not something which is within your field of competence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: No. That was not part of my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So in essence, your testimony is limited to this, isn't it, there are telephone conversations which you intercepted and transcribed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So in light of that, I'm going to have very few questions for you about some of the intercepts. But first I do want to ask you some questions about someone who lived through the siege of Sarajevo. Now, is it right that you were in Sarajevo throughout the siege?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't think it's contested that there was a terrible siege of Sarajevo in which many civilians were sniped at and shelled. Would you be able to, just in a few phrases, explain how that was from your point of view, what you experienced.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Very difficult. There was no water, there was no food. There was fire from all sides. I had to walk to work for over 10 kilometres. There was no public transportation, and I don't know what else to say. We are all trying very hard to put all that behind as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. It was simply that. As far as telephone lines in Sarajevo were concerned, is it right that there were telephone lines in Sarajevo which went -- which would go through a central or a telephone switchboard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. This is not something I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just really this: Are you aware that the Serbs in amongst the targets that they were shelling, that the telephone exchange was also a target which was being attacked in order to disrupt communications. Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. The main post office building in Sarajevo was destroyed and completely torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be right to say, wouldn't it, that it would be completely wrong in fact to have the impression that anyone in Sarajevo had easy, uninterrupted communications with the outside world?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: It was very difficult to communicate. Many telephone lines in the city of Sarajevo were not working, and as for our communication with the outside world this was really difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now just a question or two about Tuzla firstly. As far as you're aware, Tuzla was physically cut off from Sarajevo by the Serb forces. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Probably, but I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that Srebrenica was completely encircled and cut off from the rest of the world?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when we're talking about Sarajevo, Tuzla, and Srebrenica, in fact we're talking about three islands of government-held territory, cut off from each other by hostile Serb forces. Would that be a correct characterisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware at the time in 1992 and 1993 that conditions in Srebrenica were in fact far worse even than they were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I knew that because of my job. That's how I became aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that regard, if the witness could be shown P350, Prosecution Exhibit P350. And in the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is one of your intercepts. And in English it's page 3 of 7, and in the B/C/S it's page 4, which is 01752820, in fact it's 15 lines the top. This is Redzep Musanovic in Travnik apparently speaking. I just want to read this one passage. In English it says: "We are talking about reliable combatants who are not even afraid of death, but now they only want to go to Posavina in the direction of Brcko or towards Doboj or to go and liberate that corridor up there towards Bratunac, Zvornik, Vlasenica, Srebrenica. You know that men up there have been asking for help since April. They are surrounded. They have not received any aid in troops, weapons, medical supplies, or food." And this is dated 30 October 1992. It's really just to ask you this: Seeing that, does that reflect what your understanding was of the situation in Srebrenica, namely that since April 1992 they had been cut off and had been asking for troops, weapons, medical supplies, and the like, and had not received it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it right that in Sarajevo Srebrenica was infamous even in the harsh conditions of the siege of Sarajevo, but as being a place completely cut off and in a desperate situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you agree that in these circumstances and at this time, dealing with late 1992/early 1993, that communication between Sarajevo and Srebrenica was only ever very primitive? Would you agree with that description?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that regard you were referring to how when you heard a relay from Srebrenica that you could sometimes tell that it was radio because you said, quote, you "could hear the switch being made." Now, could you just explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I was talking about standard procedures for switching on to the radio line. There is a certain kind of noise. It's very difficult for me to explain after such a long time. You can hear that click, the point when the communication becomes radio communication. You know that you can hear communication via a radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't one of the features of radio communication that it was of much poorer quality than what you were hearing on the telephones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: If the line was poor, then the transcript shows a number of dots. However, if the lines were good, then you could hear the entire conversation without any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it quite common for the connection to even be lost in the middle of the conversation, and that's something which you would also mark in the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes. If the connection was lost, then we would note that by saying "connection lost."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you also aware at the time that the Serbs had receivers with which they could listen in to different frequencies and intercept phone calls between Sarajevo and Tuzla and between the radio communications with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with your superiors about the fact that these were open lines which were not secure and which could be listened to by the enemy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I did not have much contact with my superiors. We had our bosses in our department, and those were the people that we talked to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: In some of the conversations you intercepted, you would hear people saying, would you not, this line is not secure, people can listen in, and they would accordingly modify their conversation in light of the fact that it wasn't secure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: There were such cases. There were people who didn't want to say things on the telephone, and they just did not want to continue talking about those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't one of the reasons given in at least one of the conversations which you monitored that things could be overheard by the Serbs and could boost their morale or be used by the Serbs as propaganda. Is that something you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I don't remember. If you were to jog my memory by showing me a piece of paper, then maybe I would be able to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I might do that in a moment. We'll come back to that. Now, a couple of questions about voice identification. You told us how you became familiar with the voice of Sefer Halilovic because he was an object. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the intercepts which we saw where it was noted it was a conversation with Naser, that was noted because he had introduced himself as Naser?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I would like to show the witness P364. I believe in fact that probably wasn't in fact used by the Prosecution today, but it's a Prosecution exhibit. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, firstly I would just like you to have a look at that. And it's correct, isn't it, that that in fact is not -- doesn't look like one of your intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting and this is not my document, not one of my transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But you see, do you not, that it is of the same sector and department that you worked in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just -- in fact, I might just ask you a question in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could we move into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you'll look at this transcript or this intercept you'll notice it's purportedly a conversation between Sefer Halilovic -- it says: "Sefer Halilovic received a call from the centre. They have Srebrenica and Naser on the line." And then do you see that throughout this conversation S is referring to the person as 147, and in fact the person's -- the person is indicated by 147. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In none of the conversations which you intercepted was a Naser referred to as 147 by Sefer Halilovic, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this intercept is dated the 16th of April, 1993. Isn't it right that you yourself in fact intercepted a conversation allegedly between Naser and Sefer Halilovic on that very day? And it's P359.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could be shown P359. And I'm going to be working from the full English translation which we just received today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that this is first of all a conversation which you transcribed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's dated the 16th of April, 1993. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look through this carefully, and we'll do the same, in all of the exchanges between Naser and Sefer Halilovic, which starts on page 6 of 9 in the English. In the B/C/S it starts on page 13. That in none of those exchanges, and I've counted 12, does Sefer Halilovic refer to Naser as 147?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does it strike you as odd from your experience that on the same day Sefer Halilovic has two conversations with Naser, and in one of them he calls him 147 in practically every line and in the other one he doesn't call him 147 even once?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I don't know why this is so. I can't explain that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. We'll come back to 364 subsequently, although in fact there's one correction on P364 which I'd like to just deal with while we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If Your Honours give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Keep 364 available because I think we might still need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's simply this in fact. On the English version on the last page, page 8 of 8, in the second paragraph where one sees 147 and you have "I understand, chief. So God willing, we will talk at 11.00." And then it goes on to Salam, et cetera, in fact that should be attributed to S, and I think that's clear from the B/C/S version, page 14. Perhaps the witness can confirm that. It's page 14.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you see four lines down just where you see Salam, isn't it correct that in fact there's an S to the left there and in fact that's a different speaker speaking at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I know nothing of this document. This is not my document, therefore I can't say anything about it. I'm not familiar with the handwriting and I can't even read some of the words in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was simply if the witness could assist, and I think it is something we can probably see for ourselves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is obvious in fact that it couldn't be the same person speaking, all what we see in those five lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there's reference to Seba being there. I thought it was important to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we could stick with P359 for a moment. I don't know if the witness still has P359.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to draw your attention to some passages there which I want to ask you about. I'm going to read out some passages from the English and hopefully you'll be able to follow in the original. Now firstly, on page 1, we have S saying, and this is a conversation between Kemal Muftic calling Sefer Halilovic S. "My information is the situation in Srebrenica is very bad. Call him. Let's see what can be done to protect those people there." That's also on page 1 of the B/C/S. The next page, and it's page 3 of the B/C/S, S, and this is in a conversation of Ibrahim. "Are Srebrenica and lines of defence being shelled? "I: Yes, both the town and the lines of defence incessantly." And then we go on to page 3 of 9 in the English, and it's page 7 of the B/C/S. We see S there at the top there saying: "Srebrenica is being shelled. The town and the lines of defence are being shelled very ferociously, and there are very ferocious infantry attacks. You can call him again and tell him that very ferocious attacks are being launched from Zeleni Jadar and Casi [phoen]. We're asking from him that the UNPROFOR is to protect people there. He has to deem that operation very urgent, that they have to go in there as soon as possible to protect people, as the ammunition of our people is depleting." Do you see that in the original?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then two more passages on page 6 of 9 in the English a few pages over, and it's the bit we saw earlier below 080 counter number. And it's page 13 in the B/C/S where it says Naser and Sefer Halilovic: "N: As regards the situation, it is very dramatic in the area of Srebrenica. So, we are about to fall, we are about to fall. People are panic-stricken. There is still some morale among the troops. We are trying to do something. However, everything is going in the Chetniks' favour so all that you have heard is unfortunately the truth." And then turning the next page in the English, it's page 15 in the B/C/S. We see N saying: "We are stopping now" -- this is halfway down in the English. "We are stopping now because we have to observe the cease-fire. That is the condition now. We have observe it because if it's physically challenged without legs, without arms. There are about a thousand of them whom I'm not going to leave and several commanders here have their troops who are not going to leave these people. And the civilians, you know, everybody is fighting to save their own head. As regards the troops, that is still on a required level." And in fact finally I would just like to draw attention to the next page in English, which is page 17 in the B/C/S where N refers to: "To consult with The Presidency and to do that to send it." And that's a reference to sending communications. Now, in relation to those quotes, and have you seen all of those, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is one of the conversations which you transcribed. Do you actually recall -- recall the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Would you agree that the content is fairly dramatic regarding the imminent fall of Srebrenica in April 1993, so it's really a question of whether that was something which you recalled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that at the time that Srebrenica was expected to fall in April 1993 and that there were these fears that a massacre would ensue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about the appearance of the name Naser on some of these intercepts. And as we saw on some of the intercepts we see the name Naser, in others we have Naser Oric. For example, in P361 and P363. It's right, isn't it, that Sefer Halilovic only ever referred to the person as Naser. In fact, he never used the full name Naser Oric. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: They usually used first names, but whenever someone introduced themselves using their full name, both first and last, this would be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So typically Sefer Halilovic would just say Naser, and I'm looking at, for example, P361 we see that Naser is the hero of BiH state, Naser is our hero, et cetera. So it's right you never actually heard him saying Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: No. They always used names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your service aware back in 1992 and 1993 that there was a radio operator in Srebrenica who was also called Naser?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it right that in a conversation intercepted in late March 1993, that Halilovic appeared not to know basic details of who Naser was, including his surname?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if it would assist to show the witness P358.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is dated the 24th of March, 1993, and the employee, the operator, is 50144. And I'm taking it from your earlier answer that you don't actually know what the operator was for this intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the part I want to draw your attention to is from part 3, which is page 5 of 6 in the English, and in the B/C/S it's pages 9 to 10 with the ERN 01754009 to 01754010. And I'll just read that into the record: "Sefer called Hazim, illegible, because he forgot to tell him something. "S: Listen, please, I forgot. Do you have any information on Naser? "The other S: Personal data, et cetera. "S: Uh-huh. I'll pronounce it "Sh" to distinguish the two S's. "Sh: I do not have. "S: What is his last name? "Sh: Oric. "S: Are you sure? "Sh: Sure, Naser Oric. "S: He is probably the commander of the municipal staff there. Other person: Yep. "S: Did he establish some kind of a brigade there or a unit? "Sh: No, not officially. As far as I know, not. "S: All right. "Sh: Well, let me tell you, his wife came here with kids yesterday. "S: Naser's wife? "Sh: Yes. We have accommodated them in a new two-room apartment, food was provided for a month, they were accepted and so on. "S: Excellent. How many of them? The other person replies: Two children. "S: He seems to be a younger man. The other person: Yes. He's about 32, 33 years old. "S: What is his occupation anyway? The other person replies: I think that he was a policeman." I'll stop there. Now, do you agree from this that it appeared that Sefer Halilovic appeared not to know what Oric's last name was, what Naser's last name was, at least in late March 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I don't know. You're asking me about other people's transcripts. I'm afraid this is not something that I can comment on. I know about what I wrote. I know about the names I wrote. I know about the last names I wrote. That much was clear. But I'm afraid I can't comment on anyone else's transcripts. This is the first time I have seen this handwriting, whereas I am, goes without saying, familiar with my own. But I can't talk about this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. And there's no criticism whatsoever or any reproach intended. It was merely if you could assist. So that's fine. Now, a couple of more questions on another subject. Apart from voice identification of objects whose voices are familiar to you, you said that you would rely on how people announced themselves in order to say who was on the line. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it right that in fact that way of identifying someone was much more common than voice identification, in that there were very few voices which you would actually recognise; it would be much more common that you would hear someone introduce themselves and use that as the basis of who they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes. People introduced themselves. We write down their initials. If they don't introduce themselves, we put them down as X.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown an intercept which isn't an exhibit yet. The ERN number is 01757471 to 01757473. We have copies for everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, firstly would you agree that this is one of the conversations which you transcribed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes. This is my handwriting and this is my code.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is dated 4th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say as well, isn't it, that you were shown this document when you were interviewed by the Prosecution and that you signed the back of it? Not on that copy but when you were interviewed in August last year you were shown this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Probably, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, here it says, and I'm looking at the very first conversation. Zeljko Knez calls the Skup feature and talks to Emina. And if we look at the conversation, the person who's then noted with the Z, for Zeljko, claims that he can be called directly by Sefer Halilovic, in other words, from Sarajevo to Tuzla. And the woman Emina seems surprised by that and says, "That's fantastic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we carry on we see the next conversation, we see, don't we, that in fact this was all highly suspicious, because X, the man who calls Emina, says: "That phone's suspicious, don't use it." Then he says: "Do you know who called?" She says: "He introduced himself to me as Knez." And then he says: X: "You know Knez has just informed me that he didn't call anybody." And then he goes on to advise that a bit of caution is needed. Now my question about that is that despite what appears in the second half of this conversation, in other words, the doubt that's thrown on the fact that it really was Zeljko Knez, it's right, isn't it, that it's still -- the transcript still states that Zeljko Knez was the person who called the Skup feature and spoke to Emina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when suspicions or uncertainties came about which would throw doubt on whether in fact the interlocutor was who he claimed, that's not something which would cause you to rectify the transcript. It would still say that this was Zeljko Knez. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: There's no way I could know if it was Zeljko Knez or not. That's how he introduced himself and that's what got written down. And then everything else continued. This was all transcribed from the same tape, one conversation after another, and that's what you see recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And again, it's not a criticism, it's simply to make this point: That sometimes -- let me put it this way. That in the transcripts a name would appear because simply had said "I'm Zeljko" or "I'm Knez," whereas in fact it might not be that person. They simply introduced themselves that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be also right, as we seem -- as we might gather from this document, that there's a great deal of fear, suspicion, and mistrust at the time in Sarajevo and among the SDB service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I put that badly. Let me put it this way: The Ministry of the Interior at the time was intercepting the phone calls of their own army commander, the army commander of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number to be given to this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be Defence Exhibit 2?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if the witness could now be shown Exhibit P351, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, this is a conversation which was transcribed by you and it's dated the 15th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we see there in the conversation. I'll just draw your attention to certain parts -- in fact, firstly if I could, before getting into that, ask you this. You told us how Sefer Halilovic was sometimes referred to with the letter K, sometimes by the letter S. Here we see him referred to by Sl, and in fact the code Sloboda. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what in fact makes you think that Sloboda there referred to Sefer Halilovic? Did you in fact know that code name already?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I did not know the code name. This was the radio centre; that's what the transcript says, a call from the radio centre. And then probably it was said by radio that the code name referred to Sefer. I can't remember specifically, but if that's what you see here as something that was written down, then it must have been the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it somewhat confusing for your service to have three different initials which could stand for Sefer Halilovic, S, K, and now Sl as well? Is that really how it worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: It could have worked that way for the simple reason that you would have a pair of brackets with the initials of all those who took part in a conversation. And whenever there were changes that were added to the transcript, you would always have explanations in the brackets. Sk, for example, Sefer, we always had to add these explanations in order to be able to make sense of who was who.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, assuming -- assuming that it is indeed Sefer Halilovic who is speaking. We see there that he says: "Whom am I talking to? Is it AP or is it the colleague?" And So replies: "Here is the guest from the south, as ordered." Sefer then says: "Come on, say that again. And So replies: "Ptica speaking, the guest from the south." Then it goes on. There's a lengthy conversation. I would like to direct your attention to a couple of pages over, it's in English, it's page 3 or 4. And there at the end of all of it Sefer Halilovic speaks to man from the radio centre and says: "Who the hell was that?" The next reply is: "Ptica, he says. I don't know." Firstly, "Ptica" in your language means a small bird, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: "Ptica" means a bird. I'm not sure if it can mean anything else at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. So it's correct, isn't it, in this conversation that Sefer Halilovic speaks to someone at great length and pretends to know who's calling apparently, but in fact he doesn't have a clue who's been at the other end. Would you agree with that characterisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that chime with your recollection of the climate of the times, the very difficult environment of not knowing who is who and who is friend or foe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in staying with this exhibit, further on Sefer Halilovic asks if it's possible to establish the connection with Srebrenica. And I'm looking at page 3 of the English, and it's pages 3 to 4 of the Bosnian. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And he asks if it's possible to establish the connection with Srebrenica. And says: "I have not talked to them in a while." And then X then says: "Whom should we ask for there?" And he says, Halilovic: "I do not know. Ask for the chief." "The chief in Srebrenica?" "Yes. There is one who is in Srebrenica and one who is in the field." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: There is one in Srebrenica and there is one in the field, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So would you agree that in essence there Halilovic is simply saying, Take me or put me in contact with the chief, whoever that is, he doesn't appear to know who the chief is in Srebrenica at that time? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, that's something that this -- Mr. Jones is asking this witness to read into. There's absolutely nothing that this witness can utilise to ascribe that particular meaning to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, point taken. Yeah, yeah, it's okay. It's -- you're drawing a conclusion which the witness -- which isn't fair to ask the witness to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fair enough, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one final question on this conversation. We see X is the interlocutor. So firstly -- that means that's an unknown person. Correct? Unknown to you, to your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Unknown because they failed to introduce themselves at the start of conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And doesn't it also mean that that person wasn't intercepted very much, otherwise you would have recognised their voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Probably, yes. If I had a chance to listen to it frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, finally I just want to go back to P364 again briefly. And I take the point again that this is not one of your intercepts but it's simply to see if you can help us with something which appears there. I'm looking at page 6 of 8 in the English; in the B/C/S it's on page 10, starting six lines from the bottom from the B/C/S. And it's the line which in B/C/S -- it says: [B/C/S spoken], which in English is: "Naser, the people who remained in Srebrenica is a green people. And it goes on: "America does not want a green people. However, we are not a green people. We are Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is all nations, nationalities." And it's simply to ask you this on the basis of your experience. Would you agree that green people is a reference to Muslim people and that green is the symbolic colour of Islam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Again, you're asking me about someone else's documents. There is no way I can know what went on. I'm not familiar with this document. All I know about is the quote you just read out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was simply to get at this point. You worked for the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes. A Croat from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you worked alongside Serbs and Bosnian Muslims in your service. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you agree that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not a Muslim government and the ABiH was not a Muslim army, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: As far as I know, all the different ethnic groups were in the armed forces, not just Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, there are a couple of final matters, Your Honour. One is I put to a prior witness questions about the non-preservation of audio tapes. I don't feel it particularly necessary to put it to this witness, but if Your Honours deem it appropriate or necessary, I'll do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We feel nothing necessary, Mr. Jones. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Probably for good measure I should do. With the usher assistance if the witness can be shown D204.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the meantime, Witness, I can just ask you this: As far as you are aware, tapes, tape-recordings, would be preserved by being recorded on to reel-to-reel tapes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes. They would be preserved, sometimes copied on to other tapes, longer tapes. And then they would be preserved in the archive, but I have no idea how long they would be preserved for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Simply to show you the second page of this exhibit, D204. And you'll see there that your name is listed in relation to intercepted material. And you'll see that alongside most, if not all of the entries where your name appears it says nema audio, in other words, there is no audio available. And my question is this: It appears from this that there were no longer audio records for any of the intercepts listed in this document. And it's right, isn't it, that that would not fit with the practice of your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it strike you as odd, based upon the practices which you observed when you worked for the SDB, if the tapes which you transcribed were not -- were no longer preserved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Usually after a while everything that was no longer required would be erased. I'm not sure how long things were kept for. It wasn't down to us to make that call, it was down to other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we have one or two final exhibits, if Your Honours would just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, you did not put it on the ELMO that time, did you? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have copies of the new exhibit, and the ERN is 01758244 to 01758254.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, if you could just have a look at this document, and again as you'll notice straight away, I'm sure, it's not one of the conversations which you transcribed so you don't have to have any worries on that score. It would simply to ask you this: Whether firstly looking at the heading the SDB, the sector, and the department, whether from all the indications this is an intercept of the same service which you worked in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it right, even from the operator number, that that is one which is pretty close to your operator number; in fact, the next in sequence, I believe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I would seek to tender this into evidence for other purposes which don't concern this witness, but it seems this witness is the most appropriate one to introduce this exhibit. So I would simply ask for an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Jones. This will be 270, D270.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will become Defence Exhibit D270.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In fact, I have no further questions. I would simply request that, if possible, we be provided with the audio original P362, which we've noted today. There is something which we need to check. So that is something which I simply raise. And I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Just one question. Re-examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that radio communications between Sarajevo and Srebrenica were primitive. In the years 1992 or 1993, did you actually study or receive any information as to what the radio communications, if any, actually were as between the enclave of Srebrenica and Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C009
utterances.text: No. We had no information on that. All I could do was write down what I heard on the tape. If I heard that radio communications had been established, then that was what I wrote down. I had no other information on that, nor did we.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: No further re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. I don't have any questions either, which means that your testimony comes to an end here. We're finished with you. You will now be escorted by Madam Usher out of the courtroom, and the other officers of this Tribunal will extend to you all the assistance that you need to facilitate your return back home at the earliest opportunity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, on behalf of Judge Brydensholt from Denmark and Judge Eser from Germany and on my own behalf, I should like to thank you for having come over to give testimony, give evidence, in this case against Naser Oric. And before you leave the courtroom, on behalf of everyone present here I would like to extend to you our best wishes for a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's it. I take it that tomorrow you need the entire day for -- to continue proofing of the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we need to adjourn here basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, there was one matter which I thought I should perhaps remind Your Honour that you wanted to hear from us about which was Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, we can postpone that for the time being because we still haven't really discussed it amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are pretty much there already I mean, but I would rather not open the discussion before I have formalised it between ourselves, as it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, I just thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've already done what we needed to do. It's just a short meeting that we need to have to make sure that we are fine-tuned, the three of us, that's all. Then of course you will have an opportunity. Unless of course since you both come from a practical common law jurisdiction, you opt to -- for what was opted in the Limaj case and just keep moving. MR. DI FAZIO: That suits the Prosecution I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's -- we shan't be adopting that course. We are -- I might just mention that we are nonetheless in favour of an expedited procedure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, definitely. It's going to be expedited in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One matter I might just mention is that in the course of that discussion there's -- there will be a general discussion about what sort of procedure, but more concretely we may be getting into questions of dates. And in that regard it would be helpful if we could have clarification from the Chamber of when the Prosecution case closes, is it the moment the last witness leaves the room or some other event? And that's something which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it like this, Mr. Jones, there are these options. Let's start with the picture as it is projected now. Things remaining as they are, basically we're talking, according to Mr. Wubben, of Prosecution resting its case first or second day of June, which we can live with. I mean, it's not a problem. If we can advance it, then obviously we prefer it. The only way of advancing it or -- there are two ways of advancing it. One way is if those three witnesses that will be coming over to testify or are scheduled to come over to testify on the chain of custody of documents testify in-chief by means of a written statement, to be followed, if necessary at all, by cross-examination viva voce, yeah, which would shorten the trial by a few days, but it will definitely shorten the trial by a few days. The other thing is the following: Given that for the time being, we would need to decide whether we would take advantage of the few days gained or whether we would be liberal and make those couple of days available for the examination-in-chief and cross-examination of witnesses in excess of what is indicated in the document that the Prosecution has made available. In other words, we told you earlier on this week that we are pretty much unhappy - and when I say "pretty much" I really mean it - with the situation obtaining when we are told or we are told to expect witness testifying in-chief for three hours, and then we end up with that witness testifying for almost nine hours. That is simply unacceptable, unacceptable because of normal court management, exigencies, and unacceptable also because the moment we allow that witness to continue testifying for nine hours, or eight hours, then automatically we are generating a longer cross-examination. So we will be curtailing on that. We made it clear earlier on this week that if there is an indication that Monday's witness, for example, is needed in-chief for five hours, that's how long he is going to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, may -- I had less in mind the specific date on which the Prosecution case will close but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's according to what the -- what Mr. Wubben tells us, and I have no reason to doubt Mr. Wubben's word. He is extremely reliable. We will be finishing 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With Witness number 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But the point really is really this, Your Honour, it's a different point which is that, does the Prosecution case -- is it closed at that moment when the last witness leaves, or are there other events or event -- and I don't wish to enter into it because it concerns confidential matter of which we are aware, but whether it be following that event or those events that the Prosecution case would close because that has a bearing, obviously, on when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not part of the Prosecution case. That's something which has been triggered by us, not by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To me at least, and I stand to be corrected by my two colleagues, because of course you're catching me on the wrong foot here or -- to me, the Prosecution has got to do nothing with that. When the Prosecution finishes with the last witness, witness 53 or whoever that may be, basically I expect Mr. Wubben to stand up and to tell the Trial Chamber, this is where the Prosecution rests its case, or the Prosecution rests its case. That's what I expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. Thank you for that indication, because that obviously has a bearing on when 98 bis will take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Then obviously -- anyway, let's not discuss any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think I've made myself clear that that particular procedure does not form part of the case for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In my opinion. If the other two colleagues disagree with me, obviously I take that back and we come back to you on it. But I don't see it as forming part of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's something completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honours, regarding that decision you mentioned that's up to the Trial Chamber, and we will of course abide by the fact when our last witness will be -- will have finalised his or her testimony. Then we will confirm that to the Trial Chamber. What might be needed, and my learned friend also being of supportive information, is some kind of scheduling, some kind of overall addressing by this Trial Chamber when it comes to 98 bis submission. And as it will be the first or the second time done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the first time, I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, it might be the second time because there's another case. After this change of December 2004, then it might be good to have some observations, some opinions, by the parties to advise Your Honours what we think of as a kind of forum, as a kind of scheduling, to track the steps in which Trial Chamber might be able to give a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Basically I can tell you straight and plain that it will be as expedited as possible. I mean, forget about the months that used to be -- that were taken before for the motion and then for the response and then for the response to the response and the further response to the response to the response, forget all that. This is going to be expedited in this period of the amendment that was promulgated. And also, if I may say so, Rule 6 itself makes it clear when amendments to the rules come into effect. Of course, they must not prejudice the rights of the accused. And the rights of the accused are obviously not prejudiced if the Rule 98 procedure is followed according to the new regime rather than the old. I mean, rules -- the submissions for acquittal need not be in writing, in other words, for the rights of the accused to be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Our position on that is we're in complete agreement. We even thought maybe even a five-day schedule where we have two days for our motion and the Prosecution respond and we reply all in one week, and the reason why we say that is simply because this is our application. It is something which is the right of the accused, and it won't come as any surprise to the Prosecution, the submissions we make, because of course as the trial proceeds they know which evidence they think show any elements, and so there shouldn't be any -- you know, certainly any lengthy period or indeed any period, we would submit, that the Prosecution have to go away and consider our arguments because they should already know at the end of their case what they think they've proved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Basically, I mean, as I said, we haven't finalised the discussions amongst ourselves, although we have all the material ready there. The thing is this: It boils down to you will have -- although the three of us probably come from a system where the moment the Prosecution rests its case, this is disposed of almost immediately, this question of Rule 98. In my jurisdiction, I mean, it's done there and then. I mean, it's -- and you make your submissions, they make their submissions, and if I am presiding alone, I will just hand out an oral decision there and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it succeeds sometimes as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it succeeds. But the reason is -- because you will have lived the case, I will have lived the case, and the Prosecution will have lived the case; so that's the whole reason. Here, I definitely will not be suggesting to my two colleagues that everything be done on the same day as the Prosecution rests its case. I don't think we should adopt that system. So we will come back to you anyway. So -- but you can rest assured that you will have ample opportunity to prepare and present your case for acquittal under Rule 98. And same applies to the Prosecution when it comes to responding. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And if I give that a thought so there might also be time available, not only for preparing for the reply towards the submission of Defence counsel, but also we might think -- and to expedite this trial in the spirit of the change of the rule, for a kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Only in spirit. I mean, the probability or almost the certainty is that we come back to you and tell you it's the new rule that applies. I mean, in my mind there's no question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And to serve that purpose, it might also be supportive if Defence will give some notice, let's say two weeks in advance, to update the Prosecution what kind of issues will be addressed in their 98 bis submission. I mean, only the issues, not submission or clarification. Let's say when there are 300 issues to address by Defence counsel, then it is very important for Trial Chamber, both as Prosecution, to know that in order to fit in a schedule and to be decided upon by this Trial Chamber. That's an additional thought, apart from the fact that the scheduling needs really some guideline by this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I don't know how much Mr. Jones agrees with you, and I don't know how much we will agree with you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But anyway, let's postpone this discussion until we have discussed. It's a good thing that we have at least heard some of your opinions, but please do restrict and base your submissions on what we have in the rules. I know that we don't have much, but stick to the rules. Stick to the rules. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One observation, we simply couldn't possibly notify what your argument is going to be until the case is closed. That's why the submission comes at the close of the Prosecution case. In any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's postpone the whole matter, yeah. I thank you. So we will reconvene on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Monday -- morning? Morning. In this courtroom? Monday morning in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of May, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.46 p.m.,
